title: Reading a scientific paper
note: Most research articles follow IMRaD: Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. Don't read straight through. Start with the title and abstract, then study the figures and tables, which hold the actual evidence, and check the methods before you trust the discussion.

read.title: Figures first
text: A research article is not a novel. Reading it straight from the first word to the last is slow, and it lets the authors' framing shape your view before you have seen the evidence.

Start with the title and abstract to learn the question and the claimed answer. Then go to the figures and tables. They hold the data the whole paper rests on. Read each caption, note what is on each axis, and check what the error bars represent. Ask yourself what you would conclude before reading the authors' interpretation.

Next, read the Methods with a few questions in mind. Who was studied, and how many? Was there a comparison group? Were people randomly assigned? How was the main outcome measured? Weak methods cannot be rescued by an impressive Discussion.

Only then read the Discussion, and compare its claims with what you saw. Authors may lean on words like "suggests" for good reason, or they may stretch a modest result into a broad conclusion. Look for the limitations paragraph and the funding and conflict-of-interest statements. A paper you have read this way is one you can actually explain, and question.

q.q: Why does the reading recommend looking at figures before the Discussion?
o: Figures are always free of errors
So you see the evidence before the authors' interpretation
Figures replace the need to read Methods

q.q: Which question belongs to reading the Methods?
o: What do the authors hope future work will show?

q.q: What should you compare the Discussion's claims against?
o: The length of the reference list
